title: None touch it but the purified
hook: a noble Qur'an in a guarded book, touched only by the purified (56:77–79)
tomorrow: He is with you wherever you are

segments.voice: Yesterday: afara'aytum, have you seen, asked of the water and the fire. Your line was who made it?

Walk into many Muslim homes and you'll find the Qur'an on the highest shelf, often wrapped in cloth, nothing stacked on top. When someone takes it down, they may pause, go and wash, and come back. Children learn not to put it on the floor. A guest might be surprised by all the care around one book. Much of it traces back to three verses near the end of Surah Al-Waqi'ah, and what those verses mean, Muslim scholars have discussed, with more than one answer, for a very long time.

Verses seventy-seven to seventy-nine. Pickthall: "That (this) is indeed a noble Qur'an In a Book kept hidden Which none toucheth save the purified". Three things. The Qur'an is karim, noble, generous. It is in a kitab maknun, a book kept hidden, guarded. And none touches it but the mutahharun, the purified. Here the readings divide. Many classical commentators said the hidden book is the heavenly original, the preserved tablet, and the purified who touch it are the angels. On that reading, the verse describes the Qur'an's source, not a rule for people. Others read it as also pointing to the written copy on earth, the mushaf. And most jurists, whichever reading they held, required ritual purity to touch the mushaf. They leaned as well on a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to 'Amr ibn Hazm in Yemen, preserved in Malik's Muwatta: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. So the four main Sunni schools, and Shia jurists too, generally hold that you should be in wudu, the washing before prayer, to touch the written Arabic text. A minority of scholars, among them Ibn Hazm of Andalusia, didn't require it. Reciting from memory without wudu is widely allowed. Whatever the ruling, the habit it built is the one in the hook: the book isn't just picked up. It's prepared for. The washing comes first, and the reading after.
screen: `A NOBLE QUR'AN, A BOOK KEPT HIDDEN.` · `THE PURIFIED: ANGELS, SAY MANY.` · `THE LETTER TO 'AMR IBN HAZM.` · `WASH FIRST, THEN READ.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, you might make wudu now, slowly, noticing the water on hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet, then sit before you open the Qur'an. If that isn't yours, wash your hands and face slowly, with full attention, and come back to sit before whatever you read next. Let the water be the beginning of the reading.
Mutahharun: the purified, those alone said to touch the guarded book that holds a noble Qur'an, honored on earth with wudu. Today's word.
Your line: touched with purity. A noble book, and a lot of care around it. Day six hundred eleven, done.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule that you must wash before touching the Qur'an.
what it means: a verse about the Qur'an's guarded source, which also shaped how Muslims handle the written copy.

what a scholar hears: kitab maknun read by many as al-lawh al-mahfuz and the mutahharun as angels; the legal ruling also rests on the letter to 'Amr ibn Hazm in the Muwatta; Ibn Hazm's Zahiri view dissented.
